deep.reconstruction:
Context. On the previous page Riemann proves that the area of a minimal surface equals twice the sum of the areas of its images in the X, Y, Z planes. That page uses his Weierstrass-type representation x = X + X', etc., with dX^2 + dY^2 + dZ^2 = 0 and X holomorphic in eta. Here eta is the stereographic coordinate of the unit normal (Gauss map); s = y + iz and s' = y - iz. This page, headed 'Transformation der Coordinaten', begins the case where the given boundary consists of straight lines (Section I).

(1) Boundary conditions, discontinuities, branchings.
- The boundary pieces must be straight lines.
- The lines must either meet or run to infinity. In the second case the surface extends to infinity between them.
- The simplest case is two infinite skew lines.

(2) Choice of axes.
- Take the x-axis along the common perpendicular. Then x is constant on each line. The figure shows two skew lines and their common perpendicular.
- Right column: along a straight boundary line the surface normal is perpendicular to the line. The planes perpendicular to the lines contain the x-direction ('Die Ebenen senkrecht zu den Linien sind der x Axe parallel').
- At infinity the normal is perpendicular to both lines, i.e. parallel to the x-axis. It is +x at one end and -x at the other.
- So the spherical (Gauss) image of the boundary consists of two great half-circles (meridians) through the poles eta = 0 and eta = infinity.
- On each meridian the angular coordinate (arg eta; Riemann's letter is uncertain) is constant.

(3) Solution.
- Let a be the difference of the x-values (the distance between the lines). Let alpha be the difference of the angular values on the sphere (the turning angle).
- My inference: x must be linear in arg eta. Riemann takes the holomorphic part X = -i(a/2alpha) log eta.
- Hence x = X + X' = -i(a/2alpha)(log eta - log eta').
- Also s = -i(a/2alpha)(eta - 1/eta') and s' = -i(a/2alpha)(1/eta - eta').

Verification (mine). Put c = a/(2alpha) and eta = rho e^{i phi}.
- x = 2c phi = (a/alpha) phi, which is real.
- s = c(1/rho - rho) e^{i(phi + pi/2)}, and s' is its complex conjugate.
- Holomorphic parts: dX = -ic deta/eta, dS = -ic deta, dS' = ic deta/eta^2.
- So dX^2 + dS dS' = -c^2 deta^2/eta^2 + c^2 deta^2/eta^2 = 0, the isotropy condition.
- Right column: s/s' = -eta/eta'. Thus arg s determines arg eta, which determines x linearly. Riemann concludes 'also Schraubenfläche': the right helicoid with axis x, advancing a while turning through alpha.
- 'alpha = n pi + (-1)^n alpha_0': the turning angle is fixed by the geometric angle alpha_0 between the lines only up to additional half-turns. The surface may wind several times.

(4) Area integral.
- Away from the axis, x is a (multivalued) function of (y, z): x = -i(a/2alpha)(log s - log s') + const.
- With d/dy = d/ds + d/ds' and d/dz = i(d/ds - d/ds'):
  - dx/dy = -i(a/2alpha)(1/s - 1/s'),
  - dx/dz = (a/2alpha)(1/s + 1/s').
- Hence 1 + (dx/dy)^2 + (dx/dz)^2 = 1 + (a^2/alpha^2)/(s s'), with s s' = y^2 + z^2.
- The area element is ± sqrt(1 + a^2/(alpha^2 (y^2 + z^2))) dy dz.

(5) Conclusion, left column.
- The area integral is infinite, since the integrand tends to 1 over an unbounded sector region. So one cannot speak of a minimum of it.
- One must change the individual area elements by quantities independent of x, so that the integral becomes finite. Such changes do not alter the Euler-Lagrange (minimal surface) equation.
- The next page carries this out. Subtracting the projection (∓1) is still insufficient: the remainder behaves like a^2/(2alpha^2 r^2), and its integral against r dr diverges logarithmically.
- Riemann finally subtracts the helicoid's own integrand, sqrt(1 + a^2/(alpha^2 (y^2 + z^2))). This is a renormalized area relative to a reference surface.
errors: No mathematical errors in the formulas: x, s, s' satisfy the isotropy condition, are mutually consistent (s' = conj(s), x real), and the derivatives and area element are correct.
Riemann writes the first line as x = -i(a/2alpha) log eta. This is really only the holomorphic part X; the full real x is the next formula. Probably a notational slip or capital X in the manuscript.

Writing x as a single function of (y, z) is valid only locally. The helicoid strip projects onto a (possibly multi-sheeted) sector pair and is singular along the axis, which explains the ± in front of the root. This is not addressed on the page.

The rule alpha = n pi + (-1)^n alpha_0 is stated without derivation. Exactly which turning angles are compatible with the orientation condition (normal +x at one end, -x at the other) is not justified here.

results.what: Minimal surface spanned by two skew infinite lines found via the Gauss map: the boundary maps to two meridians, x is proportional to arg eta, giving the right helicoid x = (a/alpha) arg(eta) with explicit s, s'
results.modern_name: Weierstrass-Enneper representation of the helicoid; boundary-value problem with straight-line boundaries via Gauss map and Schwarz reflection
results.usually_credited_to: Helicoid as minimal surface: Meusnier (1776); representation: Enneper (1864), Weierstrass (1866); Riemann's method published posthumously by Hattendorff (1867)

results.what: Observation that the Gauss image of a straight boundary line lies on a great circle (normal perpendicular to the line)
results.modern_name: Gauss map of a minimal surface along a straight line (cf. Schwarz reflection principle)

results.what: Explicit graph form of the helicoid: dx/dy, dx/dz and area density sqrt(1 + a^2/(alpha^2 (y^2+z^2)))
results.modern_name: Area element of the helicoid as a multivalued graph

results.what: Area of an unbounded minimal surface is infinite; replace it by area minus an x-independent density so the variational problem keeps the same Euler-Lagrange equation but the functional is finite
results.modern_name: Renormalized / regularized area (subtracting a null Lagrangian or reference-surface density)
results.usually_credited_to: General idea is folklore in the calculus of variations; renormalized area in the modern sense: Graham-Witten (1999), Alexakis-Mazzeo; for Euclidean minimal surfaces various 20th-century authors

deep.surprise_reason: The helicoid as the minimal surface between two skew lines, and the Gauss-map/great-circle reasoning, belong to Riemann's posthumously published minimal-surface memoir (Hattendorff 1867). The computations are routine. The one mildly notable point is the explicit idea of renormalizing the infinite area by subtracting an x-independent density without changing the variational equation, an early instance of a regularized-area idea. Even that is a natural calculus-of-variations trick rather than a major anticipation.

transcription_corrections: The first formula after 'Hieraus ergiebt sich' appears to begin with a capital (Fraktur-like) X, i.e. X = -i(a/2alpha) log eta is the holomorphic part, not the full x.

The letter rendered 'ζ' in 'es hat in jedem ζ einen constanten Werth' and 'die der Werthe von ζ gleich α' must denote the angular coordinate on the sphere (arg eta, or an equivalent such as log eta / i). The reading of the symbol is uncertain, but mathematically it is the azimuth that is constant on each meridian.
'Die pos. Normale an dem einen Ende der pos. Lage[?]' should read roughly 'der pos. x Axe ... an dem andern der negativen parallel': the normal is parallel to +x at one end and to -x at the other.
In 'dx/dz = (a/2alpha)(1/s + 1/s')' the manuscript shows a struck-out factor (likely '-i') before a/2alpha; the surviving expression is correct.
The final right-column line reads approximately '= ± sqrt(1 + aa/(alpha alpha) · 1/(s s')) (dy dz)', with an illegible struck-out word before it.
